questions.q: In the equation \(E_{k\,\max} = hf - W\), what does the work function \(W\) of the metal represent?
options: The maximum kinetic energy of an emitted photoelectron
The minimum energy required to remove the electron from the metal surface
The energy of the incident photon, equal to \(hf\)
The frequency of light below which no photoelectrons are emitted
questions.explanation: In the energy equation \(E_{k\,\max} = hf - W\), \(hf\) is the energy of the incident photon and \(W\) is the work function — the minimum energy required to remove the electron from the metal surface. The work function is an energy (joules or eV), not a frequency.

questions.q: Applying the gradient equation \(y = mx + b\) to the maximum-kinetic-energy versus frequency line, which equation for an emitted photoelectron results?
options: \(E_{k\,\max} = hf + W\)
\(E_{k\,\max} = W - hf\)
\(E_{k\,\max} = hf - W\)
\(E_{k\,\max} = hf \times W\)
questions.explanation: Applying \(y = mx + b\) to any of the parallel metal lines gives \(E_{k\,\max} = hf - W\): the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electron equals the incident photon energy \(hf\) minus the work function \(W\). This is an energy equation describing the interaction between one photon and one electron.

questions.q: According to Einstein's light-quantum model, why is there a threshold (cut-off) frequency below which radiation will not cause the emission of photoelectrons regardless of how bright the light source is?
options: Very intense light reflects off the metal surface before electrons can absorb it
If the energy of the photon is less than the minimum energy (the work function) required to emit an electron, the photon cannot cause an electron to be emitted
Low-frequency photons travel too slowly to reach the metal surface
The metal cools below the temperature needed to release electrons
questions.explanation: The energy of a photon is related to its frequency (\(E = hf\)). A certain minimum energy — the work function for that metal — is required to cause emission of an electron. If the energy of the photon is less than this value, the photon cannot cause an electron to be emitted, which explains the threshold frequency regardless of intensity.

questions.q: Light of wavelength 425 nm strikes a clean metallic surface and a stopping voltage of 1.25 V stops the most energetic photoelectrons. The photon energy is 2.92 eV. Calculate the work function W of the metal in eV.
questions.given: Photon energy \(hf = 2.92\,\mathrm{eV}\);  stopping voltage \(V_0 = 1.25\,\mathrm{V}\), so emitted-electron energy \(E_{k\,\max} = 1.25\,\mathrm{eV}\)
questions.explanation: Using \(E_{k\,\max} = hf - W\): when the photon energy \(hf\) is 2.92 eV the electrons have an energy of 1.25 eV (read directly from the 1.25 V stopping voltage), so \(W = 2.92 - 1.25 = 1.67\,\mathrm{eV}\). This matches Sample Problem 3.

questions.q: Electrons are emitted from a surface with a kinetic energy of \(2.6\times10^{-19}\) J. The charge on an electron is \(1.6\times10^{-19}\) C. What stopping voltage will remove all of this energy from the electrons?
questions.explanation: The maximum kinetic energy of an emitted electron is found from the stopping voltage by \(E_k = qV_0\). Rearranging, \(V_0 = E_k/q = 2.6\times10^{-19}/1.6\times10^{-19} = 1.6\,\mathrm{V}\). A stopping voltage of 1.6 V will stop these electrons.

questions.q: From memory, state the four key observations of the photoelectric effect that any theory of light must explain, and identify which one the classical wave model could explain.
keyPoints: Photoelectrons may be emitted almost immediately, with no significant time delay, even if the light intensity is very low.
There is a cut-off (threshold) frequency: radiation of lower frequency will not cause emission, regardless of how bright the source is.
Increasing the intensity of the light increases the number of photoelectrons emitted per second.
The energy of the photoelectrons does not depend on intensity but does depend on frequency; the wave model could only explain that increasing intensity increases the rate of emission.
questions.explanation: Classical (wave) physics had difficulty with three of the four observations — the lack of time delay, the cut-off frequency, and the frequency-dependence of energy. The only observation it could explain was that increasing intensity increases the rate of emission of photoelectrons.

questions.q: On a graph of the maximum kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons versus the frequency of light for several different metals, what is true of the gradient of the lines?
options: Each metal has a different gradient determined by its work function
The gradient of all the lines is equal to Planck's constant, so the lines for different metals are parallel
The gradient equals the threshold frequency of each metal
The gradient is the negative of the work function
questions.explanation: When the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons is plotted versus frequency, the gradient of the lines representing different metals is the same — equal to Planck's constant — so the lines for all the metals are parallel. The point where a line intercepts the frequency axis measures the threshold frequency for that metal.

questions.q: How did Robert Millikan's 1916 work relate to Einstein's photoelectric equation?
options: Millikan disproved Einstein's equation by showing the lines were not straight
Millikan reluctantly provided the evidence confirming Einstein's equation, describing his results as the most direct evidence for the reality of Planck's h
Millikan showed photons carry both mass and charge
Millikan first proposed that light energy is quantised in packets of hf
questions.explanation: Observations of sufficient accuracy were not available to Einstein in 1905; it was not until 1916 that Millikan, reluctantly, provided that evidence. Though he doubted the physical theory, Millikan stated his results combined with Einstein's equation provided the most direct and striking evidence for the reality of Planck's h.

questions.q: Using the photon model, explain why increasing the intensity of light whose frequency is below the threshold frequency produces no photocurrent. (3 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: The intensity of light relates to the number of photons per second striking the photocell, while the energy of each photon is fixed by its frequency (\(E = hf\)). A threshold frequency exists because photons with energy less than the work function are incapable of freeing electrons from the photocell. Increasing the intensity only increases the number of these too-weak photons arriving, not the energy of each, and an individual electron cannot accept energy from more than one photon — so no electrons are emitted and there is no photocurrent, however bright the light.

criteria.descriptor: States that intensity relates to the number of photons per second, while photon energy depends only on frequency (E = hf).
States that below threshold each photon has energy less than the work function and so cannot free an electron.
Concludes that increasing intensity adds more weak photons but no electron is emitted, so no photocurrent flows.

questions.explanation: The photon model predicts a threshold frequency because photons with energy less than the work function are incapable of freeing electrons; raising the intensity raises the photon count, not the energy per photon.

questions.q: From memory, recall the mnemonic GIN for reading a maximum-kinetic-energy versus frequency graph: what does each of the gradient, the x-intercept and the y-intercept represent?
keyPoints: G — the Gradient is Planck's constant h (the same for every metal, so all lines are parallel).
I — the x-Intercept (where K_max = 0) is the threshold frequency f₀.
N — the y-iNtercept is the Negative work function, −φ; its magnitude is the work function.
questions.explanation: Comparing \(E_{k\,\max} = hf - \phi\) with \(y = mx + c\): the gradient is \(h\), the x-intercept is the threshold frequency, and the y-intercept is \(-\phi\). A bigger work function shifts the line right (higher threshold), never changing the slope — the classic trap is quoting a positive y-intercept or drawing converging lines.

questions.q: The episode describes a photomultiplier tube as an application of the photoelectric effect. What is the photoelectric step that makes it work?
options: Heat from a filament boils electrons off the photocathode by thermionic emission
A single faint photon strikes a metal photocathode and, by the photoelectric effect, ejects a single electron, which is then accelerated and amplified into a measurable pulse
Photons are reflected between mirrors until they gain enough energy to ionise a gas
An electric field strips electrons directly from the photocathode without any light
questions.explanation: In a photomultiplier tube a single faint photon ejects one electron from the photocathode by the photoelectric effect; that electron is accelerated onto a series of plates, knocking loose more electrons at each stage, amplifying the signal a million-fold so individual photons can be detected. The marks come from naming the photoelectric step, not just the device.
